Supply-National Revenue SUPPLY
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Rea in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE Customs and excise divisions-
259. General administration, $4,089,027.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Before this vote is discussed, Mr. Chairman, I presume the committee will expect a short statement from me. As the committee well knows, there are two divisions in the Department of National Revenue, customs and excise on the one hand and taxation on the other. We have now called one of the items with respect to customs and excise, and I shall speak briefly on that division at the moment. After the committee has seen fit to pass the votes in connection with that division I shall again speak briefly on the taxation division.
This division, customs and excise, administers not only the Customs Act, the Customs Tariff, the Excise Act and the Excise Tax Act, exclusive of part I, but also administers many other acts with which most hon. members, I am sure, are familiar. The division administers in whole or in part, for instance, the Immigration Act, Export and Import Permits Act, the contagious diseases act, and altogether there are over 40 statutes or acts in addition to the general ones in which this division of the department has to play some part at one time or another.
In so far as the organization of the customs and excise division is concerned, there are 24 branches here at headquarters in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Order; I wonder whether hon. members would lower their voices, because we cannot hear the minister.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Some of these, such as excise audit, investigation, drawbacks, inspection and personnel, have field offices throughout the country. Then, of course, there are the ports, the outports, vessel clearing stations, some 435 in all, which run one might say the length and breadth of this country and are situated at border crossing points, coastal and inland points, airports and so forth. Packages imported through the postal service, all alcoholic and tobacco products manufactured, are under the supervision of the officers of this division. All licensed manufacturers who have to pay either sales tax or excise tax are visited by our auditors and have their records checked and liabilities to the department determined.
I suppose the general public usually thinks of the customs officer as a man in uniform whom they see at the airport or at a particular port of entry. Of course there are also a substantial number in addition to

Supply-National Revenue those men who are employed by the department. If one takes the fiscal year 1953-54 as a basis of comparison to show the work that is done by this division, I would say the total number of import entries processed during the fiscal year 1957-58 increased over 1953-54 by 564,920 entries or 16.58 per cent, and the increase in revenues collected totalled $203,168,000 plus.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: What was the year?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
The year was 1953-54 as compared with 1957-58. That is an increase in revenue from that division of 11.7 per cent. During the same period revenue from the excise tax increased by $44 million plus or 19 per cent, and within the area of international travel the number of vehicles entering Canada carrying Canadians and Americans increased by over 4 million or 30 per cent.
It should be remembered that every person, vehicle, ship, aircraft, train, truck and automobile which crosses our borders or enters our harbours or airports is subject to customs control. Therefore as the country grows and prospers the work involved in collecting revenue and providing essential customs services increases, and of necessity the staff required to ^carry out these functions also increases.
At this point, and because salaries, wages and overtime together account for something like 92 per cent of the total estimates for customs and excise-$35,892,047, to be exact-I should like to say a word or two about the staffing policy of this division. To put it simply, it is a policy of maintaining strict control over all personnel establishments to ensure a flexible organization that combines economy of administration with operational efficiency. Toward this end, efficient establishment control procedures have been established on the basis of extensively developed work formulas and standards, and these are used in conjunction with a system of statistical reporting and the recommendations of our organization and methods unit from studies of work procedures and practices now in effect at the various ports throughout the country. In other words, in simple language, we study the record in order to know where increases and decreases are taking place.
This makes it possible for the establishment control unit at headquarters to keep in close touch with the work situation at every port in the country, and to maintain up to date information concerning any significant change in the normal business index of a port, information which can be translated immediately into terms of proper staffing needs.

It is from those ports which show a fairly well established decline in business that staff is transferred to fill a need elsewhere, whenever it is practicable to do so. On the other hand, positions which become vacant at a port where the trend of business is downward are also transferred, or earmarked "not to be filled" unless specifically authorized by the headquarters establishment control unit.
I presume that I will be saying something on the individual votes as they are called. I shall attempt to answer questions after we have had the questions and opinions of the members of the committee. At the moment I think this general statement is sufficient, and we will now deal with the individual matters.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I want to thank the minister for his statement. I must say that this is the first time he has been before the house on his estimates, though he has been minister for 14 months. While he is very familiar to the committee this week, I am sorry to say he was not before the committee last year with his estimates. I will not digress into that subject, but I am one of those who have very strong views about the action of the government last year in not bringing the estimates before the committee for approval in the usual way under the British parliamentary system, but rather choosing to deal with them by governor general's warrants in a way that I regard as wholly improper. However, I will not digress into a debate on that point here.
The minister has had 14 months in which to familiarize himself with the department. Bearing in mind the fact that he was not before the committee last year with his estimates, I hope today he will give us as full information as he can about the operation of the department. I think he will find that his department is a well manned department, and that generally speaking he has an excellent staff. I am sure that is what he found when he took office on June 21, 1957. It is sometimes rather difficult to separate the two divisions of this department, but I should like to ask the minister one or two rather general questions. I think perhaps this is the point at which to do so.
I am one of those who have always held the view that the headquarters of the department are quite inadequate, in relation to the important work it has to do and the volume of work it has to do and the number of members of the public who have to be interviewed. I should like to ask the minister if he cares to comment on this point, and in particular if he has taken any steps to

procure more adequate housing in Ottawa for the headquarters of his staff.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: There is no question but that the space occupied by the department is taxed to the very limit. Negotiations were going on before I became minister with respect to the acquisition of other property immediately adjoining the Connaught building, but these negotiations did not bring forth the result which the officials hoped they would. Representations have been made to the Minister of Public Works, however, and the hon. member is certainly perfectly correct when he says that additional room is required by the department and will have to be obtained within the very near future.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Not only is it a matter of the working efficiency of the staff being impaired as a result of the inadequacy of their quarters, but there is also the difficulty of persons coming to the department to discuss particular customs entries or items, particularly those under the excise tax, and having to carry on those discussions in a room occupied by as many as 40 or 50 persons and as close as six, eight or ten feet to other taxpayers who are discussing their problems with other officials.
I know the officials are very careful with respect to this point, and they do all they can in the circumstances; but in view of the difficulties faced by the taxpayers in these circumstances, particularly the danger of disclosing processes concerned with the manufacture of some items, disclosures which might easily arise when arguing about what item any particular entry should come under, this is a particularly difficult problem. I have in mind the danger of disclosing to a competitor information which is ordinarily regarded under our system as private information belonging only to the particular taxpayer, and as this difficulty is so great I hope the minister will continue to press the matter and that he will find a solution. I do know something about the proceedings in this regard before the minister took office, though I am not in the position of knowing anything about them since. However, I hope this very important subject will continue to receive his attention.
I have one or two specific questions which I would like to ask. Could the minister give us the comparative number of ports, out-ports and preventive stations for the last three years if he has those figures conveniently at hand. I would like to see if there is any material change one way or the other.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I will have that for the hon. member in a moment, if he will proceed.
Supply-National Revenue

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
At the same time I would like to ask him to give us the information which he has available up to the latest possible date covering the entries of motor vehicles from other countries. I am not referring to imported vehicles but to tourist and business vehicles being driven into the country by citizens of other countries and then being returned. I would appreciate having any statistics he could give us on that matter covering the last three years.
I would also like him to give us the information he has for the last three years, and for as recently as he has it available, concerning the amount of excise tax collected on new automobiles manufactured.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will answer those questions a little later on.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, because I do not know under what heading I should ask these questions I should like to ask them now, and perhaps the minister would answer them at this time or on the appropriate items. Can the minister state whether there has been any increase in the activities of his appraisal staff with regard to dumping duty, and what has caused that increase? If there has been an increase, to what extent has the increase taken place? I might tell the minister I have had some dealings with that branch of his service and have found the service excellent and the officials highly co-operative and very much on their toes; but I also found the activities a little more intense than in the past, and I would appreciate it if the minister could tell us why that activity has been intensified and to what extent.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to dumping duty specifically, or the valuation and appraisal work of the appraisal department?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Generally there seems to be an increased tempo of activity in the valuations, which of course we will discuss under the item that will come up a little later. There has been some concern expressed as to why there has been increased activity.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
The increased activity has resulted because of investigations which have been made of importations coming in and specific inquiries referred to the department for investigation. The hon. member will know that during the early part of the war a great many of the senior members of the organization staff were absorbed in other branches of national service. At the end of the war through promotions many were absorbed elsewhere. There was a tremendous shortage of trained staff, particularly in the appraisal section. This was also caused by the great industrial development across the

Supply-National Revenue country and the full employment and boom that followed the war. Therefore it was some considerable time before it was possible to recruit the staff that was desirable.
As the hon. member knows, steps were taken toward that end some time ago, and when I came into office I saw that they were carried out. We have advertised, and as we shall show later in the discussion concerning the appraisal section 46 new appraisers have been authorized by the civil service commission. Some of those positions have been filled, and we are filling others as rapidly as possible to carry out the increased work load which has been put upon the department because of the development of the Canadian economy.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Another question, Mr. Chairman. I wonder whether the minister could put my mind, at least, at ease on this question. I was apprehensive that perhaps with the advent of a new government imports were perhaps being managed administratively rather than legislatively. I had some doubt about the matter and wondered if the desire to make imports a little more difficult was responsible for the increased activity. I should like to have the minister's comment on that point.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there has been no change in administration whatsoever except, as I said, that staff vacancies have been filled. There have been an increasing number of complaints from importers and Canadian businessmen with respect to what they alleged were violations of the Customs Act. After all, in the years following the war there was a field day so far as business was concerned. There was no trouble with the Customs Act or anything else. People were ready to buy. It was only during the last two or three years that complaints started to come in and the work load increased tremendously.
As I said, the staff was not there to meet the increased work load. My predecessor had started to increase the staff to take care of it, and we have been carrying on. There has been no change whatsoever in the administrative practice, but because of the increased staff we have perhaps been able- and I hope we have-to investigate the complaints and deal with them more efficiently than was possible before, not because we are more efficient but simply because we have the increased staff.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister whether the operations of the United States customs simplification act and the

whole question of United States administrative protection are his concern, and do they come under his jurisdiction?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: That is a matter more for the officers of finance, but we also have communication and discuss these matters.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: If so, could the minister state if the operation of the United States customs simplification act has removed, and to what extent, the complaints we used to have about administrative protection interfering with our exports to the United States?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while this item is before the committee I should like to bring to the minister's attention a matter which is of very great importance not only to my constituents, the majority of whom are fishermen, but to all the fishermen of Newfoundland. Coming from the maritime provinces, the minister will understand that shore fishermen are dependent entirely on a supply of bait. He will also understand what a cod jigger is. That is the particular kind of hook shore fishermen must employ to catch fish when no bait is available.
All through the history of Newfoundland, prior to confederation and since, fish hooks and jiggers of various kinds used for commercial fishing have entered the country duty free. A couple of years ago when there was no bait the people of the maritimes and Newfoundland learned about a new type of cod jigger which had been developed in Norway, and which had been tried out and found to be much more efficient in the catching of fish than the kind of jigger that is usually employed. Unfortunately this particular type of jigger is called by the Norwegians a lure. The only part of it that resembles a lure is a little piece of red plastic which is interspaced between the hook and the weight; but because of their being described as lures these jiggers have been subject to customs duty of 20 per cent plus sales tax of 10 per cent, which has served to make the cost practically prohibitive to the fishermen who require them so badly.
This may be only a matter of the interpretation of the act, or a matter of judgment on the part of the appraiser. I have an illustration of this device which I would like to pass to the minister so he will know what I am talking about. I do hope that he will take whatever steps are necessary to have this particular type of jigger reclassified so it can come into Newfoundland and the maritime provinces free of duty.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to look into it, Mr. Chairman, to see whether it is a matter of interpretation. From sad experience I find that everybody who writes me about

changing the tariffs says it is simply a matter of interpretation, and that I can wipe it out entirely. Unfortunately the Minister of Finance takes a far different view. As the committee well knows, the Minister of Finance, under the law of this country, is responsible for taxation policy. It is my unfortunate job to have to administer the act. After the longhaired boys of finance evolve their philosophical findings, then we do the work; but I shall look into this, of course, and if it is a matter of administration I do not have to tell the hon. member that my sympathies would be entirely with him and the maritime provinces.
The hon. member for Ottawa West asked about ports, outports, and so on. There are 435 ports and outports at present, and I am told there has been no significant change in the last three years. There might have been a change in one or two, but it is within that range within the last three-year period.
We have no figures giving the number of tourist cars or United States cars coming into Canada. We simply have cars coming in and, unfortunately for the purposes of the hon. member, these will include Canadians returning to Canada as well as United States residents coming in. For the calendar year 1956, 17,341,800 cars came in. That was a 30 per cent increase over 1953. In 1957, the last year for which we have the complete figures, 17,982,400 cars came in; in other words, an increase of about 500,000 motor vehicles between 1956 and 1957.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Has the minister any figure as to how it is running this year?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
We have not those figures available yet.
The Leader of the Opposition asked me a question with respect to the customs simplification practices of the United States government. Mr. Chairman, my remarks have to do with a particular matter concerning the customs and excise officers of the Department of National Revenue at the

harbour of Montreal. I am informed that as of July 1, 1958 these officers of the department were notified that all overtime work would be compensated for by time off, and that section 86 of the civil service regulations would be applied to them by the minister. Section 86 makes that provision. I believe it is also the common practice in all departments of the government for the officer in charge to decide whether or not to apply the rules strictly. In any event, I am not suggesting now that cash should be paid for all overtime work at all levels of government employment and that section 86 of the civil service regulations should be repealed, though I would think that in due time we should give serious consideration to the matter.
But I think the government is making a great mistake in compensating for overtime work by allowing time off in departments where it was the accepted practice to pay employees in cash for such work. Because of the nature of his duties the employee has to incur expenses for meal and transportation charges which are increasing all over the country at the present time. Yet he is not paid in cash, though it has been the practice to do so for over a decade. I think such a change in policy kills the incentive of the employee, and the minister will agree that it is not a morale booster for the staff especially at this time, in view of the fact that since June 1, 1957 the cost of the most essential items of shelter, clothing and food, has increased.
At the harbour of Montreal this change in policy affects at least 110 employees. I think the minister will agree that companies are charged for the extra work done by the officers of the department, and that these revenues come to the department. Therefore I think it is only fair that we should continue to pay the employees in cash.
The minister will appreciate that no recognized union in this country would tolerate a private industry paying its union members for overtime work by allowing time off. Instead of getting rid of this antiquated rule, why does the government now try to extend this bad system of paying employees with time off? The employees generally disapprove of such a system, and I think they are on very firm ground in criticizing the change in policy.
When the minister was on this side of the house he advocated that in our relations with our civil service employees we should try to treat them as much as possible along the same lines as private industry treats its employees. The minister is now getting far away from the common rule in private industry, where employees are paid in cash
Supply-National Revenue for extra work. We know the minister is administering a very important department, that he needs revenue and that his officials are always on the job to see that duties are paid to the last cent. This is sound and good administration. If the minister, for example, were claiming an amount owing by a farmer, surely he would not like to be paid with a bag of potatoes. The same rule applies to his employees. The department asks them to do extra work and instead of paying them in cash gives them a piece of paper entitling them to a holiday. I should like to ask the minister two questions. Is there anywhere in his estimates an additional amount to pay for such overtime work in cash? It appears that by reason of a decision of the Department of National Revenue these port employees were notified that as of July 1, 1958 all overtime work would in future be compensated for in accordance with civil service regulations and not paid for in cash as was the case prior thereto. There are, I am

Supply-National Revenue informed, 110 employees at the port of Montreal who are affected by this decision. They have made representations to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and to me. These representations are made, let me assure the minister, in a most respectful manner, asking him to reconsider the case because of the conditions which have been outlined by the previous speaker.
It has been pointed out that the decision taken by the department is one which is going to have a demoralizing effect upon the officers, in view of the hardships they will suffer because of the fact that instead of receiving cash which has been an incentive for overtime work they will now be in receipt of compensatory leave for work done. They believe that an officer who, because of his duties, has incurred extra expenses such as meals, transportation costs and the like as a result of overtime work, may have a feeling of resentment which is understandable. In their opinion this method is unfair and unjust, since the officer is being penalized when he has to work under these more difficult circumstances because he is no longer in receipt of cash but time off as compensation in lieu thereof.
It is brought to my attention also that if such compensatory time is accumulated in the winter months, it is not much use. If they are paid such overtime in cash, their families and the communities in which they live benefit; their purchasing power is increased, and they are able to meet conditions of life more advantageously than they otherwise would. It is pointed out to me that the effect of this decision is that it cuts by one-sixth, in some cases, the purchasing power they have hitherto possessed. It is my understanding also that the cost of this extra work is, in most cases, charged against the companies accommodated and therefore brings revenue to the department. They feel this is a point which should be given consideration when the question of cash for overtime is under study.
I realize that for years, as has been stated so clearly here, the practice of the administration has been to pay for overtime in cash only when the work load has been so heavy that overtime could not be compensated for in leave. In the port of Montreal, because of the circumstances which exist there, particularly in the eight months of navigation where the work load is not of an ordinary nature but of an extraordinary nature, it seems as if it were a deterrent to the increased efficiency in the national revenue staff. I know, too, that the administrator of the port has a certain discretion in a matter such as this, but I am wondering if I could not be so bold as to say [Mr. Chevrier.l

that perhaps that officer has exercised his discretion in a manner which may in effect be detrimental to the efficient operation of the department.
Without saying more, I wonder if I could not prevail upon the minister and his officers, efficient as they may be, who are before him now to give consideration to this case. It is working a hardship on these 110 employees. The withdrawal of this cash allowance which has been in existence for the last 10 years, as has been stated so well by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, seems to me a bit severe. Will the minister, therefore, under the circumstances and having regard to what is happening in the port of Montreal and the overwork that exists there, not reconsider this matter so these men may be placed in the same position as they were prior to this decree coming into effect?

Perhaps I should deal now with this matter to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and the hon. member for Laurier. They suggested that we should provide remuneration for overtime by virtue of section 86 of the Civil Service Act, and that is exactly what has been done. I am advised that section 86 of the Civil Service Act makes it mandatory that overtime should be paid for by compensatory time, if that is available, and only if it is not available should cash be paid.
Now, there was a very wide departure from the provisions of section 86. The hon. member for Laurier referred to the discretion of the port administrator. He has a discretion, and he also has a responsibility.
I am sure that hon. members will not argue that there is more business being done at that port than there was last year, but the overtime in the month of May of this year amounted to $16,000. This was twice as much as was paid a year ago. As the result of a port audit by the headquarters staff, they compared the figures and found they were going up steadily, so they suggested there should be a stricter enforcement of section 86 of the Civil Service Act. As a result, in the month of June the amount was reduced to $8,800 for overtime, although business had increased somewhat in the month of June over the month of May.
This is a problem which has caused great concern to all the officers. One wants to use discretion and one appreciates the arguments about hardship, but I do think there are some cases in which overtime has been paid. I am not speaking now of Montreal at all; I am speaking of a port of which I have knowledge much nearer my own home, where a practice has grown up of paying cash for overtime.

We find year after year more and more overtime being paid and no compensatory time being allowed. If the act is to be changed, that is a matter for the government and for parliament, I suppose; but that is the law as it stands at the moment.
I certainly will take a look at this particular case, and naturally will give it every consideration. However, I think those are the basic facts, particularly respecting that month of May in which there was such a startling increase of $5,000 more than any other month last year. That was something the auditing authorities thought should be brought forcibly to the attention of the responsible officers in Montreal, and that they should be asked to see how section 86 would work. As I said, overtime then was reduced to $8,000, and still gave compensatory time for the balance.
I was also asked about the amount in the estimates, if any, for this overtime. There is $900,000 included in the estimates this year for overtime, which is $200,000 more than it has ever been before. It can therefore be seen that this is a problem. I think all hon. members can realize the difficulties in connection with its administration. It varies with collectors, ports, personal relationships and so on. You get problems of administration which are not the easiest to deal with. However, we must do it in the best way we can. Certainly we might pay more overtime and reduce staff.
It must be remembered that in the winter time many of these people have very little to do, but nevertheless they are carried. There was a time when you paid overtime in the summer and let them go in the winter. However, that policy was found to be unsound and was changed by the preceding administration, and I think properly so. But that is the crux of the problem. Those are the facts in so far as Montreal is concerned. It is a problem which affects not every port but a good many of them in this country, and is one which is receiving careful attention.

I want to read just briefly from the editorial. It is headed, "Keep Border Open all Night". This gentleman's name is Denis Williams, and he will be pleased to know that I brought his views to the attention of the minister. After his reply to the representations made by two hon. members who spoke previously I enter this arena with considerable hope. He writes as follows:
Attempts to persuade the national revenue department to maintain a 24-hour service at the Paterson border crossing have been in progress for years, and Ottawa's uncompromising attitude is disclosed in the following letter we received from Kootenay West member H. W. Herridge at the week-end.
I took the opportunity to send him a letter, knowing of course that he was a supporter of the government. He goes on to say this:
We think that Mr. Sim is missing the point. He is mistaken if he believes there is no value

in keeping the Paterson customs office open just because the U.S. authorities decline to maintain a 24-hour service at Northport.
It is not southbound traffic that we are concerned about. We are interested primarily in the plight of Canadians who want to return to Canada and cannot do so if they arrive at Paterson after midnight.
At present, West Kootenaians visiting Spokane, for instance, must time their departure in the evening in order to arrive at Paterson before the witching-hour. If they fail, they are put to the inconvenience and expense of spending the night in the U.S. Similiarly, Trail citizens week-ending at Christina lake must leave Laurier by 10.30 at the latest if they expect to spend the night in their own beds.
Most of them do so in our constituency.
Then there are dozens of travellers who head east through Osoyoos and the Sherman pass rather than endure the discomforts of the Greenwood to Rossland section of highway 3; and they too must plan their schedules to bring them to Paterson before midnight.
The operation of Paterson on a 24-hour basis would prove of the utmost advantage to hundreds of Canadians-wanting to get back into Canada. To these people, the hours of business of the U.S. customs and immigration office at Northport are of no consequence, since no clearance is required by the U.S. authorities in order for a Canadian to leave Washington.
Mr. Sim says that his department's observations indicate that the increase in hours beyond midnight could not be justified "by the amount of traffic operating through the port during these hours."
Here the deputy minister is on shaky ground-
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I very seldom find the deputy minister on shaky ground.
-to say the least. How can he possibly calculate the amount of traffic that would enter Canada after midnight when he refuses to keep the border post open? The fact is, of course, that a large number of drivers who now either spend the night in the U.S. or time their arrival at Paterson before midnight, would use all-night facilities if they existed. One cannot tell what the volume of traffic through Paterson might be once it was generally known that one could enter Canada at any hour, but we believe it would be heavy.
The deputy minister's letter to Mr. Herridge rather indicates that departmental thinking in this issue is faulty. There is no relationship, as far as we are concerned, between the hours of operation of the Paterson post and the Northport U.S. office- except for people entering the United States. We think Mr. Sim might study the plight of those who use U.S. highways to avoid bad Canadian roads and who want to get back into Canada to suit their own convenience.
I just read that because I do think it points up some of the reasons for the argument very well, and I would urge the minister to take another look into this question because of the rapidly growing traffic between the United States and that part of British Columbia which I have the honour to represent.

Apparently, this company obtains heavy equipment such as cars, diesel engines, trucks, tractors and the like from the United States government. Apparently this equipment is used in Japan and elsewhere. The equipment is refurbished and rebuilt. Sometimes it is brand new equipment which has not been used but has been declared surplus by the United States government. It is turned over to the Golden Gate Equipment Company. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there have
been numerous discussions between the Minister of Justice and myself with respect to this rather difficult and nasty task, one of

which I was unaware until I came in and I found on my desk one morning a heterogeneous collection of what might be called books -at least they were books; I would not say there was any resemblance to literature- and then I realized what a minor task there was in this department. I said I would have nothing to do with it, as I thought there was a better way to deal with it. Out of that arose those discussions with the Minister of Justice.
No final decision has been taken. Various alternatives have been discussed. As the hon. member points out, the Minister of Justice can take action with respect to domestic matters in this country, but I am afraid there is still going to be responsibility on the customs authorities in so far as importation is concerned, because all imports have to go through our offices. It is impossible to give any suggestion as to the time spent on this matter. The procedure, as the hon. member knows, is for a book or a box of books, or whatever it may be, to come into a port, and the collector there, the customs officer or whoever it may be, has to examine them. If in his opinion they offend that section as being treasonable, seditious, immoral or salacious and so on, then he sends them to his next senior officer, the collector. If he still thinks they are in that category they are then sent to the head office in Ottawa and the assistant deputy minister and the executive assistant take a look at them. I do not know when they do this reading. I imagine most of these books are such that they would not want to read them at all. If they decide that they are in that category they then go to the desk of the deputy minister, and if he feels that they fall within that category they finally arrive on my desk. A decision has been made on the way up the line, and I have to concur in it or otherwise.
It is impossible to say how much time is spent. I certainly have not spent a great deal of time on it. There have not been very many crossing my desk. During the last few months I have seen very few, but that is the way the machinery works. It is unsatisfactory, and it does not guarantee any great control. The officer may happen to be busy or he may be the type of man who has a very liberal outlook. If so, he will say, "This book is all right; I will pass it". Another officer may have a different view of these things.
Perhaps I should not say this, but I can think of one example to show how it works. Last year I had submitted to me six lithographs for inclusion in this year's calendars. They were six nudes. They had been passed on by all these officers. Three of the nudes were absolutely nude and three had some sort of diaphanous wrapping around their
Supply

National Revenue bodies. One of the senior officers said the three which had the diaphanous clothing could be admitted because they were semi-clothed. Another officer said their posture was indecent and they should not be admitted, but the nudes could be admitted because their posture was not indecent.
That is an example of the judgment that has to be exercised and the kind of artistic skill that has to be passed upon by customs officers. I really think that we are much better qualified to deal with increasing the seasonal tariff on cabbages and cucumbers than to pass moral judgment on literature coming into the country. Heretofore any decision made could be appealed to the tariff board, but very few appeals were taken. We are all aware of one rather famous appeal a short time ago, as the result of which a certain book was admitted on a split decision of the tariff board after the department had refused it admission.
The tariff board certainly does not want to be shouldered with this task. I do not think that the tariff board is necessarily the best judge of impurity in books and literature. Perhaps I could say that the courts are not either, but someone has to take the responsibility. There will be a provision in the bill which will be before the house shortly, and I think it is a step in the right direction, providing that in future appeals from decisions of the department, if there are any, will go to a court rather than to the tariff board.

I will answer that question in a moment. I should like to make a general statement on the income tax division before we deal with the detailed questions and answers, and while the officers from that division are coming down to the floor.
By any standards, the taxation division operates a large-scale business. Last year collections in this division exceeded $3 billion. Individuals paid about one-half of that amount and corporations roughly the balance, with succession duties of about $65 million being thrown in as a sort of balancing item.
The detail work is tremendous. For instance, in 1957 returns were received from 5J million taxpayers. That figure included about 100,000 corporations.
Ledger accounts are maintained for about 130,000 instalment payers and 200,000 employers remitting tax deductions. In addition, accounting action has to be taken or was taken last year in about 700,000 cases where taxpayers declare tax owing and find that additional sums have to be assessed. Really, when one considers these figures, he gets some idea of the detail work which has to be done by the officers of this division.
The division employs 6,200 regular personnel in its 29 district offices and its head office. These figures are rather interesting. In 1937 the division had 1,214 employees and it handled 439,000 returns or an average of 362 returns for each employee. In 1947, the division had gone up to 7,400 employees and it handled 3,338,000 returns or about 450 per employee. By 1957 the number of employees was reduced, came down to 6,195 with an increase in work load, with 5,428,000 returns


or an average of 876 per employee as compared with 362 to which I referred 20 years previously. Of course, accounting machinery and improvements procedures accounted to a substantial degree for those changes.
I want to give full credit to the taxation officers for their continuing efforts to reduce expenditures and for the efficiency of this department. If time permitted I could give the figures. I put them on the record once before, showing the cost today of collecting $100 as compared with the cost a few years ago. A comparison is really amazing.
I have one qualification to make on this question of efficiency. I think it is fairly well known-it is no secret-that I have been very critical of the public relations of this department. I was critical when I sat on the opposite side of the house and I have been critical since I came over to this side of the house. When I say "of this department" I am speaking specifically of this division. It was my feeling and it is my feeling that in their zeal for efficiency they have tended sometimes to lose sight of the individual and I think there is a natural pressure to look upon the taxpayers en masse impersonally, not as people. Perhaps it is difficult or impossible to look upon them as persons, but I still think that something in that direction can be accomplished. As a result, as is well known to the officials here in front of me and the senior officials in the department, we have had many conferences on this score. Some very frank talking has been done and much thought has been given to this matter. I have received much co-operation from the officials and I think that real progress has been made, or at least I hope so. Reports would indicate that at least some progress has been made in that direction. I have at least told my officials that progress should be made in it and I know that they are attempting to make and I believe have made effective changes in that direction.
Having said that by way of criticism, I think this also should be said about the efficiency of the department. I do not know but I suppose every employee may feel this, whether he is an employee of a bank or what position he may hold. I do not know of any employees who have greater pressure brought to bear on them than have the employees of the Department of National Revenue generally and perhaps particularly the taxation division where they have to go out to people's homes, go to people's offices, interview them, conduct investigations and often are in a position in which, if they wanted to take advantage of it or of the opportunities which are presented to them, there could be a marked impairment of the efficiency of the department and a reflection on the character of the officers

themselves. I think it is a real source of satisfaction-it certainly is to me as minister, and I am sure it must be to members of parliament and of Canadians generally-that so little has ever happened which would indicate in any way any derelection of duty or any impairment of efficiency on the part of the thousands of officials who are, as I say, conducting these onerous, responsible and unpleasant tasks, often under conditions which present difficulties in connection with efficient operation.
Canada can be very proud of the calibre of its public servants, their integrity and their efficiency. There have been minor derelictions of duty in the past, as is well known, but these have usually been publicized and have been rigorously dealt with. If, as and when any occur in the future the same thing will happen, but they are so insignificant in number and in frequency compared with the operations which are carried on that I think it is worthy of comment and should be put on the record.

Mr. Chairman, any diffidence that I may feel about bringing up the Premium Iron Ore case again is really dissipated by my recalling that in the house the minister told me that some of my arguments on a previous occasion could be easily corrected or, as I recall it, he said that they had no legal basis. Therefore, I am glad to be back at it again to give the minister an opportunity of clearing up once and for all any misunderstanding there may be on this case from the point of view of this department. I suppose the matter is relevant to the Minister of Finance and also to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
A complete review of the case is hardly necessary but there are several points in question that might very well be settled now.

I might begin to make this point by reading two editorials, one from the Winnipeg Tribune of Friday, July 25, 1958, and the other from the News-Chronicle of Saturday, August 2, 1958. The editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune is entitled:
These questions should be answered.
One of the questions mentioned in chats between Prime Minister Diefenbaker and President Eisenhower during the Ottawa visit was the Premium Iron Ores case. Mr. Diefenbaker confirmed this in reply to a question in the commons.
Ordinarily the court case between Cyrus Eaton of Pugwash and the United States tax collectors would be a private fight and no particular concern of Canadians or the Ottawa government. But some of the circumstances about the case make it very much the concern of Canadians.
In the first place, the tax treaty between Ottawa and Washington seems to be jeopardized by the persistence of the United States revenue department in trying to collect taxes from Premium Iron Ores.
Washington tax collectors insist that there has been no official protest from Ottawa against the raid on Premium. Members of the Ottawa government insist that protests have been lodged repeatedly during the past several years.
To end any doubt on this question the dates and nature of the series of protests should be officially tabled in the House of Commons.
In the second place, there have been persistent reports that bureaucrats in the Ottawa revenue department have encouraged their counterparts in Washington to ignore Canadian government protests and to press the suit against Premium in the United States courts. The name of J. G. McEntyre, deputy minister of national revenue, has been repeatedly mentioned in these reports.
These questions should be asked and answered:
Has McEntyre encouraged Washington tax collectors to make a dead set on a Canadian company in spite of Ottawa government policy and the tax treaty?
Is this encouragement still going on?
If so, what does the Diefenbaker government intend to do about it?
Are United States tax officials still being supplied with information from tax files by Canadian revenue officials to help them in their case against Premium?
I would like to move from this editorial to what is perhaps a stronger editorial and at this time I am not identifying myself with either of these particular views. This is from the paper in my home town of Port Arthur, the News-Chronicle of August 2, 1958. The editorial is headed:
Matter of tax policy.
The plight of Premium Iron Ores Limited, which faces a multi-million tax suit in the United States, has been set out in these columns several times in recent months. The company, operating in Canada, and subject to Canadian taxation laws, is seeking immunity from taxation by the United States government on the basis of an agreement between Canada and the United States that was designed to prevent double taxation.
The strange feature of the case is that the heads of government appear agreed that there should be no double taxation. Official protests have gone to Washington from the previous and the present Canadian governments. Prime Minister Diefenbaker

mentioned the case to President Eisenhower during the latter's recent visit to Ottawa, and the president apparently agreed Premium was being subjected to double taxation. Why then, does the United States internal revenue department persist with the case?
The only logical answer is that high-ranking civil servants are handling the case in defiance of their superiors. It has been charged that Canada's deputy minister of national revenue and the acting head of United States revenue department have exchanged letters on the Premium case. If statements attributed to the Canadian civil servant are correct, then it is high time the government stepped in and cut him down to size.
What is involved in the Premium case is not routine business between Canadian and United States revenue departments. It is strictly a matter of policy. And policy should be made by the federal cabinet not by deputy ministers.
Prime Minister Diefenbaker should call an investigation into the Premium case to determine exactly what has gone on, and how many other cases there may be which have been decided by civil servants. It should be unnecessary to spell out duties and limitations of authority to such responsible people as deputy ministers, but the investigation may reveal such action is necessary.
Certainly it is desirable that this case, once dismissed by a United States court and now before the United States court of appeal, should be settled. If the settlement is anything other than dismissal, the position of American investment in Canada is in grave danger, and therefore so is the future of Canada.
These two editorials, I think, probably place the case much too strongly and they stem from part of the pressure campaign that has been organized by Mr. Eaton. I have no comments, pro or con, against Mr. Eaton's pressure campaign.
I think he may tend to practice it more because the American environment he has been in for so many years is more open to that and I think he may not be aware that this is rather unusual in Canada. But there is nothing to stop him from mounting such a campaign and when one considers that in a sense his own company and his own fortune are in jeopardy

I would not say his whole fortune, of course-one can understand his particular reason for being worked up about it. I have a letter from Mr. Eaton dated July 15, 1958 referring to the correspondence which has excited these newspapers. That correspondence can be found in sessional paper No. 204 containing a copy of all correspondence and other documents exchanged between the Minister of National Revenue or any officials of the department and officials of the United States concerning Consolidated Premium Iron Ores limited from January 1, 1948 to May 12, 1958. I want to read the pertinent part of Mr. Eaton's letter into the record. I do so in order that we may be able to see the situation in the opinion of one of the persons involved, a person who has been organizing his case in every possible way. He says:
Supply-National Revenue The McEntyre correspondence discloses the shocking situation of a deputy minister making confidential commitments with a foreign government in defiance of his own Prime Minister and cabinet. Some of the letters written in 1958 are self-serving documents for the record that probably were arranged by telephone calls or conferences between the writers.
I might interpolate that Mr. Eaton seems to have a suspicious mind. He goes on:
We will produce the statements from Americans to verify every line written by Judith Robinson.
This is a reference to item No. 5 in the sessional paper which was a letter to Mr. McEntyre dated April 2, 1958 from the United States treasury department over the signature of O. Gordon Delk, acting commissioner. In this letter Mr. Delk says:
The statements made in the letter of February 15, 1958, apparently have their genesis in the same source which inspired certain articles by Judith Robinson appearing in the Toronto Telegram under dates of February 18 and 20, 1958. The article of February 20 attributes the statements in question to Mr. Harry Swanson, our director of international operations, in alleged testimony on February 14, 1958, before the committee on foreign affairs of the United States house of representatives. It is assumed, therefore, that Mr. Swanson is the individual referred to in the letter which came to your attention.
Then this letter goes on to dynamite the substance of the points made by Miss Robinson in her column. Mr. Eaton says in his letter:
We will produce the statements from Americans to verify every line written by Judith Robinson. The senate and house in Washington would promptly put an end to this clear cut case of circumvention of the tax treaty between Canada and the United States, if it were not for the fact that the U.S. revenue agents continually emphasize that Canada has never protested but that on the contrary the U.S. agents have had the continued co-operation and support of the Department of National Revenue in Ottawa.
Before I put on record my own interpretation of what we might call the McEntyre correspondence I should like to put on the record the point of view expressed by the United States ambassador to Canada on April 8, 1958. In a press release issued from the United States embassy he said:
The United States department of justice has taken an appeal to the United States court of appeal against the decision, handed down last April, of the United States tax court in the tax case against Consolidated Premium Iron Ores Limited. Because of a crowded docket, it is understood that the case will not be argued until after the court's summer recess.
I understand, by the way, that the case is going to be heard in September.
The department of justice stresses that an appeal is available as a matter of right to either litigant in such cases. If either party is still dissatisfied after the court of appeals hands down its decision, either will be able to apply for certiorari to the United States supreme court. Appropriate legal remedies are similarly open to litigants in Canada.

It is also the position of the department of justice that a reversal of the tax court decision by the court of appeals would have no effect on the standing or validity of the convention between the United States and Canada for the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion in the case of income tax.
It seems to me that is the key point and that the minister might clear it up. I refer to the point made here that even if the decision does go to the United States tax authorities it is not a contravention of the double taxation treaty. The release goes on:
The tribunals of both the United States and Canada will from time to time be required to decide what the facts are in a given case and then apply pertinent provisions of the tax convention.
In all such cases it may be confidently expected that the nationals of each country will be afforded the fullest protection of the law. The United States government is vitally interested in the double taxation convention. There are no grounds for allegations that abrogations, derogation or circumvention of the convention can result from full and open consideration of the convention in the course of the Consolidated Premium Iron Ores case.
The minister is aware that as a result of this press release Mr. Merchant was taken over the hurdles by a subcommittee of the United States senate. Very severe criticism was meted out to him for issuing this statement in which he said that no matter what happened in this case the double taxation convention was not in question. If that is so, I certainly think we need a statement on the matter because I have here the brief of the respondent to the United States court of appeals and I should like to read a section of it. On page 71 there is the following:
As we have discussed, the present appeal in the Eaton and Daley cases and the Premium case is essentially a challenge to the careful, detailed factual findings and conclusions of the tax court, based upon a voluminous record of testimony and documentary evidence.
The events with which this case is concerned involved a Canadian enterprise. It concerned the production of iron ore badly needed for war purposes. The physical difficulties in exposing the ore under Steep Rock lake were enormous. The accomplishment of the engineering task, the financing and the arrangements for marketing the ore-located, as it was, in a remote wilderness-was a feat of tremendous proportions.
The transactions in these eases have at all times been subject to the taxing power of Canada, and the taxes levied by Canadian law have been and are being paid.
The effort of the internal revenue service also to subject Premium, a Canadian corporation, to United States taxes, and, as a result of a belated afterthought and an involved, elaborate, novel and devious theory, to tax United States stockholders of Premium for certain alleged profits of the Canadian corporation, is directly contrary to the treaty and to the applicable statutes, judicial decisions and ruling of the treasury department itself, and to the facts.
That, of course, is a biased point of view. It is the point of view of the respondent, but it does make the point again, as a result of


what went on before in the tax court, that despite what the United States ambassador has stated, there is a question of the double taxation convention being abrogated, and I certainly think anyone reading the last protest made by this government to the United States government would also get that impression. I should like to ask the minister to make a statement that will clear up once and for all the position of his department and the government with relation to this case, to try to give us an assessment of the protests made to the United States authorities and some indication why no action has been taken to cancel this appeal.
On the matter of the strictures upon the deputy minister that have been made by the press with regard to this particular case I think that perhaps they have been most unfair to the deputy minister and in assessing this correspondence I certainly have difficulty in deciding whether to criticize or to praise him or to be able to say whether or not he has taken the right course. I know there are some statements in there that surprise me as coming from the deputy minister, but I do not know whether or not this is normal. I have somehow the feeling that this correspondence reveals that civil servants, in their relationships with other countries, tend to behave somewhat like Chinese mandarins in one of the older dynasties, where everything was very formal, and there seems to be a feeling that the emperors, in this case the politicians, do not really know what they are about.
I would appreciate it very much, and I think we could avoid a lot of this voluminous editorial writing, I might call it, that has been going on all across Canada if the minister would make a statement to clear up these questions.

I believe, Mr. Chairman, it would be highly inappropriate for me to make a statement in detail on a matter which is presently before the United States courts. Some of the material which the hon. member has read to us this afternoon and which, as he says, is prejudiced material, suggests that this company was doing business only in Canada. Well, of course that is the crux of the case, and that is the point that has been referred to the United States courts. If the company was only doing business in Canada, then it should not be taxed in the United States. The tax authorities in the United States say it was doing business there. They took the case before the tax courts, and they lost it. For some reason, which I regret, they saw fit to take this case farther, and so far as I can tell now, may have the intention of proceeding with it. If that is their intention, there is nothing the

government of Canada can do to stop it. It is the right of their government to take matters before their courts which arise within their country. When a decision is evolved it will be a matter of very careful consideration by this government, by our officials, and then a course of action that may be necessary can be determined. Nothing more can be done in connection with this matter than has been done.
The preceding government sent an aide-memoire to the state department in Washington. Then, as the hon. member well knows, there were whispers going on, or so it was said, to disregard it; that it was not forcibly presented to the United States government. The present government sent another note to the United States government because there were many factors involved in this case as well as the tax convention itself. This government felt, for reasons which were known to the United States authorities as well as our own, that the matter should be dropped. To reinforce that, the Secretary of States for External Affairs, when he was in Washington, was instructed by this government to inform the officials of our position. I was advised that this had been done verbally to the secretary of state, the United States treasury officials and the attorney general of the United States.
When the President of the United States and the secretary of state were here a few weeks ago there were conversations with the cabinet. After the cabinet meeting, the President, the Prime Minister and I had a discussion on this matter. I am not suggesting that the hon. gentleman was misleading in any way, but it is not correct to say that the President or the secretary of state expressed an opinion on this matter. They did not say that they felt the thing was being wrongly handled or that they should not proceed with the case. I raised this, and said it was a matter of concern to the Canadian government. This time, I can vouch personally for the fact that there is no validity in the statement that this has not been communicated to the United States officials, definitely and firmly. A great deal has been said, and a lot of misinformation has been spread around, which is not justified in any way, shape or form by the facts, about civil servants communicating information from one country to the other. If any one of the persons who made this charge ever looked at the tax convention between the United States and Canada he would find that the tax convention requires the officers of one tax department to communicate to the officers of the other tax department information which is requested about the affairs of a taxpayer whom they are investigating. In other words, if information was communicated, and I believe it was in the earlier days at least by officials of national revenue, either through Mr. McEntyre or his predecessor as deputy minister or some assessor in Toronto where the file was kept, to the United States officials, that was proper. The United States officials had a right to ask for that under the terms of the tax convention and we could not have refused to give them the information, even if we had wanted to do so. Therefore, there was certain information requested and certain information given.
There was an allegation also that Mr. McEntyre had encouraged these proceedings, but the hon. member for Port Arthur had the file produced and tabled in the house, and he says quite frankly, having read the file, he cannot see any justification for these charges which have been made against Mr. McEntyre. Neither can I. I am satisfied that nothing has been done by Mr. McEntyre or by any of the other senior officials of the department, except what has been done in compliance with the terms of the convention.
I might say the hon. member asked if any information is being given by the department now. There has been no communication with the United States authorities for a long while. I presume the reason is that they have completed their investigations and do not require any further information. At any rate, they have not asked for any more information and there have been no communications from Mr. McEntyre or any other official of the department for some time. Many allegations have been made, but I am not going to stop to discuss them all now, and I certainly do not want to discuss the case itself. I do think there has been an over-emphasis, and I express it that way, of the distortion by bureaucrats and matters such as that. Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks on item 263, taxation division. I also wish to put forward a suggestion whose implementation would, I am sure, be of very great service to those taxpayers in the medium income bracket.
Before the last world war, Canadians crowded into large metropolitan centres where they expected to find work more easily.
During the war our industries developed at a very rapid rate. The population of our cities and towns increased. Then a change came over the living habits of town dwellers, who sought to quit large urban centres to establish homes in the suburbs, at distances which, at times, reached 15 or 20 miles from the cities.
It followed that those fellow citizens of ours who live on the outskirts of cities must travel considerable distances in the morning and the evening, at great expense.
If that expense is a small matter on a daily basis, the fact that it is a daily occurrence makes it very heavy to bear. People travel by bus, train or private car.
Let us take the case of a working man who lives approximately 20 miles away from his place of work and who uses a car as a means of transportation. This means that he has 40 miles to travel every day. It will be understood that, only for gas, he will have to spend at least $1.00 a day. If he works 50 six-day weeks, he will spend annually, on gas alone, $300. Add to this the wear and tear of the tires, minor repairs, insurance and depreciation. A very conservative estimate-and of course in my mind
Supply-National Revenue the word conservative is not that which is applied to the hon. gentlemen opposite- would put that expense at $600 or $700 per annum.
In my opinion it would be only fair if, for income tax purposes, the working man could deduct all his travelling expenses to and from his place of work, whatever his means of transportation.
In fact, the Income Tax Act should be amended so as to grant a tax exemption to every taxpayer for expenses incurred by the use of automobiles or other means of transportation in the performance of his work or for travelling to or from his place of work.
Workers, professionals, businessmen and manufacturers should benefit from such exemptions on the same basis as directors of large corporations.
Indeed, I am sure that directors of large corporations, in many cases, register their automobiles in the name of their company and the expenses involved are charged to the company, thus reducing profits and taxes at the same time. If a corporation director, whose annual income is substantial, is glad to be able to save a few hundred dollars on income tax, how much more the ordinary worker and, generally speaking, any Canadian who gets an average income, would appreciate an exemption for his travelling expenses by any means of transportation for the purposes of his work.
It would be mere justice to all Canadians, and I respectfully submit to the minister that he should take this suggestion under serious consideration.
While being fair to everyone, this would at the same time provide an additional means of checking the recession which we are now facing, since it would leave several millions of dollars in the hands of Canadians thereby increasing their purchasing power.
I therefore respectfully submit this suggestion to the minister in the hope that he and his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), will think it proper to consider it favourably. The same applies to their travelling expenses, airplane, train and ship tickets, and hotel accommodation, etc., which are all put on the company expense account.
I admit that, considering the profit of those corporations, the savings so achieved,-if I may use this expression,-are negligible, but to my mind, there is a principle involved.
If this principle is valid for the directors of large corporations, in all fairness, the government of Canada should grant similar advantages to all Canadians, without exception.
