speechtext: I thought that the Minister of National Revenue would suggest that the hon. member for Dollard should repeat his speech on the estimates of the Minister of Finance. I think that would be a very good idea.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
In the opening remarks of the minister under this section I think he stated that over 5,000 prosecutions were launched against delinquent taxpayers or taxpayers who had failed to file returns. As a member


of parliament I regard that statement as rather alarming and I think that parliament should give some consideration to the statement. I do not know the exact figure but it was over 5,000.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: That is for failure to file.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: For failure to file.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I will give my hon. friend the actual figures now. There were 5,000 plus prosecutions commenced but 2,200 were dropped. I suppose by "commenced" is meant the laying of the information. There were 2,200 dropped and 3,157 were actually taken to court.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Perhaps the situation is not quite as alarming as I thought at first. I feel that as members of parliament we should be concerned about the fact that 5,000 Canadians were summoned before the courts for being delinquent in making their returns. I do not know how that figure compares with past years.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I only have the figure for the immediately preceding year in front of me. In 1956-57 there were 6,100 prosecutions started and 3,126 were taken to court, or almost exactly the same number. Roughly 600 more were started the year before than last year.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I have had some experience with the department in dealing with these matters and I have found great anxiety on the part of the officials to do everything possible before a prosecution is instituted. I think the officials of the department should receive credit for that. They exhaust all possibilities, grant all the interviews that are necessary, receive all possible explanations and even grant terms for the payment of arrears of taxes. Nevertheless I feel that further study should be given to the matter not only because of the cost to the country of lodging 5,000 criminal complaints but also because of the great inconvenience and time lost. I suggest to the minister that some kind of study of the situation be instituted and perhaps we can reduce the numbers still further in the years to come.

Item agreed to.
Income tax appeal board-
265. Administration expenses, $107,130.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I want to say a word about the income tax appeal board. I have written the minister on this matter with particular regard to one special case. I want to bring the minister's attention to the fact that sometimes the income tax appeal board only sits in the larger centres and there are persons living in more isolated places who want to make appeals and who, in my opinion, are

occasioned unnecessary expense and inconvenience. I urge that every consideration be given to persons living in the smaller centres who wish to lodge appeals and who have to go to considerable expense in order to go to Vancouver or some larger centre.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I think the hon. member will remember that some change was made in his constituency or at least in his province. I sent a letter to the acting chairman of the board and arrangements were made for an additional sitting at another place. Wherever that can be done conveniently and efficiently I am always willing to give it consideration and try to work it out although obviously it involves additional expense. Sometimes matters have gone too far in that arrangements have been made, staffs have been moved in and papers brought in with the result that it cannot be done, but it will be done wherever it is practical.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I appreciate the minister's consideration but unfortunately when the board was supposed to go to Nelson the railroad was blown up, the cloud ceiling was too low for planes to fly and the bus did not get there in time for the case to be heard.
Item agreed to.
53. Grant towards the anticipated operating deficit of the radio and television services, $39,135,000.
Is the minister going to make a statement?

No. I thought I had made enough statements about the C.B.C. during this session, particularly during the last two days, and that I might be forgiven for not making a preliminary statement at this time.

The question I want to ask has to do with one I placed on the order paper some time ago with relation to radio relay stations. I happen to have more of them in my constituency than there are in any other place in Canada and we would like a few more. There are a number of communities of the necessary size to justify it. One of them is larger than some of those that now have such stations. It is very difficult to get a satisfactory statement from the C.B.C. with regard to when they are going to introduce them. I thought by asking a specific question I might be able to get a useful answer. In the estimates now before us is there an item for a radio relay station in the town of Manitouwadge?

I would rather deal with such questions when the officials are here but I am afraid I have to give the hon. member
Supply-C.B.C.
a negative answer to his question. Perhaps we could let it stand for a few minutes.
In view of the fact that we have already had two days' discussion-
And two nights.

-on radio and television broadcasting in Canada and in view of the minister's commitment that we will have a committee on the subject in the early stages of the next session of parliament, which it is beginning to look may not be too far distant, we can forgo general remarks.
There are some questions of a particular nature that we would like to ask, and perhaps the best way is to take the questions one by one. I wanted to ask the minister, first of all, about accommodation in Ottawa for the headquarters of the present Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. He will recall that some months ago there was a great deal of publicity in this city, including some photographs, of a proposed new building on a site on the Bowesville road. I wonder if the minister would tell us exactly what the situation is with respect to headquarters accommodation in Ottawa?
Has the hon. member other questions at the moment?
Well, we could take them one at a time.

The situation in connection with the headquarters building in Ottawa, Mr. Chairman, is that the moneys are included in the estimates for that building. Plans have been prepared, so I am told, and have been completed for the construction of that building. By plans I mean architect's plans and specifications. All that work has been done, and it is just a question of deciding when the building itself should be started. I think the feeling has been that in view of the other pressures on the C.B.C. there has not been too much attention given to that in the last month or two, and also with the employment situation, that it might be well to defer until later this fall the actual commencement of the construction of the building. I cannot commit the corporation definitely to that, but it is my expectation that the work of construction will be started within the next few weeks.
Has a site been chosen as yet, and if so what is the site?
Riverside drive; I think there is a big sign there saying that this is going to be the location.

There has been a good deal of controversy and a great deal of conjecture

Supply-C.B.C.
about it, so I think it is perhaps well to clear it up in an authoritative way.
The other point is this: Will supervision of the building be under the public works department or will it be under the control of the corporation itself?

The corporation has had
architects retained and plans prepared. It has been the policy of the corporation in the past to superintend its own buildings, and I would expect that practice would be followed in this case.

I should like to ask the minister about implementing some of the recommendations of the Fowler commission in regard to centralizing T.V. and radio broadcasting facilities in Toronto. I understand that there are now a dozen or so separate buildings and installations in Toronto, and that in the interests both of economy and efficiency it would be better to have them centralized in one building. I should like to ask the minister whether there has been any progress in regard to that matter and, specifically, whether the government has taken an option on a property in Don Mills, and whether that option has lapsed? What is the present position in regard to this matter?

It was expected that the corporation would be buying land at or near Toronto this year and provision has been made to that end in the capital budget. Investigations have been going on with respect to various properties in and near Toronto, and in view of the operating position of the corporation with the large number of properties we are leasing, something over 20, and with the very high annual rental, I would hope that the investigations would be completed and that the property could be acquired in the very near future. Then we could proceed with the construction of a central property. At any rate, we think we have sufficient money available this year in our capital budget to buy the land, if such land is available.

I had a specific point, and I asked whether the option which was taken on a particular property at Don Mills was taken with the approval of the government, and if so whether it has been taken up or whether it has been allowed to lapse? If so, what was the cost of the option?
Does the hon. member mean the capital cost of the land which was included in the option or the cost of getting the option?

If I could get the information on both, I should like it. How much would

this land have been on which the option was taken out? What was the cost of allowing the option to lapse if it, in fact, did lapse?

There was more than one parcel of land included in this property to which my hon. friend referred as the Don Mills property. There was a definite option taken on two properties, one owned by the Don Mills Development Limited or corporation, and the other by Famous Players Corporation. Roughly, the properties were about the same area, I think both slightly over 15 acres each, making around 31 acres in all. I have not the figures in front of me concerning the division of the option price between the two, but I can get that information if the hon. gentleman requires it. The total option, I think, although I am not certain, was $710,000 for the two properties, and the division between the two was roughly the same.
Has that option been allowed to lapse?
That option has lapsed.

Can the minister explain to the committee why that was done, when an option was taken? Is it true that the government had decided this was a reasonable proposition and had made a decision to take up the option and build on the property?

The government had taken no decision whatever, as I recall it. There was a submission and recommendation made to the minister to authorize the payment of the money to these two firms. This matter got as far as treasury board, I think, and then from there, because of the amount involved and because of the varying appraisals, I asked for additional appraisals. We had one appraisal, and frankly I was not satisfied. We got other appraisals and they varied substantially in amounts, some being over the option price and some being under the option price, and in view of the amount involved and the fact we were not going to preceed with construction just now, the option was allowed to lapse. An investigation is being carried on with respect to any possible alternative sites in the general area of Toronto.

The minister is well aware of the fact, owing to his near residence to me in this house over a period of some 11 years, that I have repeatedly urged the necessity of some low power relay stations to serve the requirements of some 3,000 people in the northern part of my constituency who, up to date, have been denied adequate radio facilities. I will say since the minister took office his department has secured estimates of the cost of providing low power relay

stations at points on the Arrow lakes near Nakusp, places on the Slocan lakes and Balfour. Can the minister inform the house if provision has been made in these estimates for the building of these low power relay stations?

There is no specific amount allocated in the estimates this year for the relay radio stations to which the hon. member refers. The C.B.C. is giving consideration, of course, to the extension of this service. In various parts of the country, as many hon. members know, there is constant pressure on the corporation to build these stations, to increase their number. It would depend upon the other expenditures which the corporation feel must be made this year under their budget as to how far they can continue to expand these relay stations. However, it is a matter which technically has developed a great deal during the last few years, and is one in which the corporation plans on extending service within the relatively immediate future.
May I ask the minister whether he has made any decision with regard to a satellite station in the Ottawa valley about which I spoke to him yesterday? He said that he might answer today.
Is that with regard to the Pembroke station?
Yes.

I should like to be able to tell everyone that all these stations are going to be built this year or at least not later than next year. However, I am not in a position to do that. With regard to that particular station which he has mentioned, I can assure the hon. member that the challenge there, shall I say, or the problem there is receiving careful consideration by the corporation. They have made a fairly intensive study of it and there is more work to be done. I hope that in the not very distant future the hon. member will be able to see the evidence of that work which is now being done.

I should like to ask the minister whether he has any statement to make in connection with the standards of television programs originating in the studios of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The other day I intimated that some programs were not satisfactory to and did not meet with the approval of some of my constituents. I attempted to read an editorial which had a particular program in mind and I was prevented from doing so because apparently I was out of order. Will the minister now permit me to read the editorial? If there is no objection I wish to read the editorial in
Supply-C.B.C.
full. This editorial appeared in the Fort William Times Journal and reads as follows:
Last week the World President of Rotary visited Fort William. He is an American from Milwaukee, an idealist who heads an international organization devoted to the cause of building goodwill between peoples of all nations. Warmly received here, the distinguished gentleman radiated friendship.
At the same time he was being welcomed in the city, laborers in the vineyard of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at Toronto were putting the finishing touches on a production which was waved into the living rooms of Canadians from coast to coast on Saturday evening.
In the name of comedy Duffy and his supporting actors staged a scene in which a cigar-smoking, "smart" American from Milwaukee browbeats an innocent Canadian. The latter comes out of a supermarket, arms loaded with parcels, to discover that the Milwaukee man has crashed into his parked car. The American, abetted by a brassy wife, is shown bribing a witness, feeding the poor Canadian shopper with whiskey from a flask before the police arrive and generally making comments that would make the average American shudder.
Behind the direction of C.B.C. productions there seems to lie an inordinate dislike of the United States and Americans. Saturday night's exhibition was no isolated example. Digs at our neighbours have been sprinkled liberally through the programs of the last year.
It is one thing for the Canadian government to take issue with the government of the United States on a specific problem, or for Canadian spokesmen outside the ranks of government to speak their piece. It is quite something else for a government-sponsored agency such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to stir up antipathy against a host of American citizens who do not deserve any kind of a spanking from tin-pot, irresponsible "artists".
That is the substance of the whole thing on which I attempted to make a statement the other day. I wonder whether the minister has in mind something of a regulatory nature that will prevent such productions from being viewed by the people of Canada. That is something that we should like to know. Our people are very much interested in what comes out of the television sets in their own living rooms. Television can be a wonderful thing for the promotion of goodwill, education and entertainment. It can also be something else. It can be a definite detriment if it is not handled and controlled properly. I should like to know what action, if any, the government intends to take.

It is rather hard to answer specifically a question like that. Certainly the government is proposing to take no action whatsoever with respect to it. What action the board of broadcast governors will take on matters of regulation is something we shall leave for them to determine. It is a matter for experience and judgment.
It is perhaps an unfortunate matter that this little skit happened to take place when prominent American people were in town. I can quite understand that the hon. gentleman is somewhat exercised about it. But

Supply-C.B.C.
after he raised the question the other day, or tried to do so, I checked on the matter. This program was on a national network, and I thought that if this thing was so bad we should see just what the audience reaction was. It must be remembered also that there would probably be more Americans than Canadians or at least just as many Americans as Canadians listening to the national television network. Naturally one would assume that there would have been many injured feelings.
We have checked in all the offices where our national television stations are located. In Halifax there was no reaction; not one came in. In Toronto we had three telephone calls, two saying it was wonderful and one saying that it stank. In Winnipeg we had no audience reaction. In Vancouver none whatsoever. In Montreal, none. That was the reaction across Canada. We had three telephone calls and one letter; and as I said, two were saying it was wonderful and two were critical of it. When you have a situation such as that, reaction can be critical but I do not think that by regulation of any kind you could control or define a situation where a show did not evoke any more reaction than that, I do not think it would be one that could be dealt with even if a board wanted to. I do not think this is an area in which boards can deal in any event.

On this point, Mr. Chairman, I suggest there is no accounting for tastes and that there never will be agreement on matters of taste. It is true, of course, that television programs not only have an important effect on public opinion within the country but they can be an important factor in relations between countries. We all appreciate that importance. I am one of those who get a great deal of pleasure out of the C.B.C. television programs. I also get much pleasure out of some of the programs we bring in from the United States. We discussed this matter at some length yesterday, namely the Canadian content of programs and the importance of that kind of thing. Since that discussion took place I have had the pleasure of reading an article by the Minister of Trade and Commerce dated July 6 for the Boston Sunday Herald. As it bears on this point perhaps I might quote just two sentences from this article by my hon. friend's colleague. Regarding our relations with the United States he says this:
We have drawn closer together in cultural matters, with Canadians sharing many of the tastes and interests of their American friends.
Canadians are reading more American magazines and seeing more American films and television programs than ever before.

And then he goes on:
The Canadian government's policy has been directed towards giving Americans the same opportunities in Canada as are given to Canadians.
I hope my hon. friend is not going to apply that particular principle to television.
I am afraid I did not catch that remark.

In so far as the Minister of Trade and Commerce is concerned, he said that the Canadian government's policy has been directed towards giving Americans the same opportunities in Canada as are given to Canadians and that was said within the context of television programs, films and magazines. I express the hope that it will not be applied to television in Canada.
It will not.

I am reliably informed that shortly before March 31 the hon. Minister of Transport-and he is in the house and is able to confirm whether my information is correct-promised to provide immediate television service at Flin Flon, Manitoba. I am just wondering whether the minister can tell the committee whether this service has been provided or whether it is the intention of the department to provide it in the relatively near future.

No, this television service has not been rendered, Mr. Chairman, and with all due respect to the hon. gentleman I do not think the Minister of Transport promised that it would be. I happen to know something about this matter, not from the Minister of Transport but because this problem has again arisen in the last few weeks. There were promoters from the United States who-
Surely the Minister of Transport is not going to leave the committee when we are discussing what he said.

-were telecasters using a substitute for microwave on the telephone lines and who wished to do this in Manitoba, as I recall it. They wanted a chance to prove whether this system could be substituted for the microwave and asked to be allowed to develop the system in Manitoba. I have seen the correspondence in this matter and the Minister of Transport at that time told them that if this could be developed it would be a very cheap way to establish television in Flin Flon and in many other areas. They were asked to go ahead by the government of Manitoba and they went ahead and just before the election, as some hon. members here may know, the government of Manitoba entered into an arrangement with them for that very purpose,

but I am told that when they attempted to carry out this proposal it did not work out satisfactorily at all. I believe, however, that the former government of Manitoba was intending to carry on experimental work in that direction. Whether or not the present government so intends I do not know but I believe that is the matter to which my hon. friend refers.

I want to ask the minister, in connection with the programming of the C.B.C., what plans have been made with respect to the program "The Nation's Business" and whether the introduction of two C.B.C. correspondents into the gallery of this house is a preliminary to the establishment by the C.B.C. of its own television correspondents in Ottawa rather than handling the matter, as at the present time, by farming the work out to various members of the press?

I had thought that possibly when we were discussing item 54 I would like to bring certain matters to the attention of the committee and of course of the minister responsible for the providing of funds to the C.B.C. from this parliament. I now wish to raise a situation which is becoming of increasing concern to the people whom I represent in the constituency of Churchill.
The hon. member who has just sat down mentioned the situation at Flin Flon. I do not now intend to launch into a throne speech, because I know I would be called out of order if I did so at this stage of the session. However, there are certain aspects I must mention about my constituency in order to bring out my point. My constituency comprises roughly 180,000 square miles, taking up almost three-fifths of the province of Manitoba. The matter which is of greatest concern to my people with respect to television is that at the present time there is not one single square mile of that area which is serviced by C.B.C. television. There are many other matters which are of interest and which have been discussed with C.B.C. officials, but when representations have been made to the C.B.C. respecting the possibility of servicing this area, we have often been told that we are too far removed from existing C.B.C. network facilities. This is not quite so, because the more largely populated areas of my riding, particularly those of Swan River, Flin Flon and The Pas, are not so very distant from existing facilities. When one speaks of the far north it is a different proposition altogether, but in regard to Swan River, for instance, which is a large agricultural area, it is only a matter of possibly 175 air miles from Winnipeg and less from Brandon. Extensions to the populated areas of
Supply-C.B.C.
Flin Flon and The Pas would probably necessitate covering some 375 miles, so it will be seen that it is not right for the C.B.C. to continually say that Churchill is too far removed from present facilities. The people of the area believe, and I think justly so, that as they are being taxed in the same way as anyone else in Canada, therefore they should share in the benefits provided by such facilities as the C.B.C.
As a result of recent correspondence and discussions, the C.B.C. informs me that until the present time no private applications have been received for television station licences in the area. Undoubtedly that is correct, but I do know of one or two private concerns who are interested in going into this area but before setting up stations they would like some idea as to just when the C.B.C. network would be available to them. The area in which I live, namely, Flin Flon, as well as other Manitoba areas, are to a large extent sports minded and, as in the case of the rest of Canada, are interested in seeing such live network programs televised by the C.B.C. as the world series, the Grey cup, the Saturday night hockey games and so on. They would also like to receive the national news service.
Some of these station operators feel that if they were to go in on a private licence and to operate with kine recordings this might just serve as a deterrent to the C.B.C. ever coming in and giving them a network.
These are the problems facing people interested in applying for private station licences, and I would like to suggest to the C.B.C. that the mere fact in itself that we have an area from which we have as yet not received applications for television licences, is a direct challenge to the C.B.C. to give serious consideration to servicing such areas in order that it may become a truly national body. In areas already serviced by private stations there is not the same degree of need but in areas where there are no private stations and where no applications have been forthcoming I believe there is a direct obligation on the C.B.C. to give this question full consideration.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister answer my questions at this time?
Would the hon. member repeat his questions? I believe he was asking a question about a specific station.

I asked about the situation with respect to "The Nation's Business". I also asked if the C.B.C. has any plans to in-stal a permanent C.B.C. correspondent who will appear somewhat in the way Stanley Burke does at the United Nations. The other question related to the prospect of installing

Supply-C.B.C.
low power relay stations at Manitouwadge and Armstrong. In both cases I made representations. In one case I sent a lengthy petition to the chairman of the C.B.C.

At the moment there is no thought of arranging for a correspondent here. I think that is a matter to which consideration will be given but there is no immediate decision forthcoming on it.
As far as "The Nation's Business" is concerned plans have been finalized to start that next month, I believe, or at least in the immediate future. It will come into being again in the fall and winter months.
The hon. gentleman can rest assured that the problem to which he referred is well along in the planning stage. I would not want to suggest he could expect developments there this year in the construction line at any rate but I would be hopeful that in another year real progress could be made in helping to solve the problem which I know is a difficult one. The C.B.C. is faced with a tremendous problem. It has moneys which though large in total amount are small when one thinks of the number of requests that come to it from all over Canada for the construction of power relays, new stations and things of that kind. It has had to try to deal with the problem on the basis of the funds available, on the basis of need and on the basis of the investigations of the officials of the Department of Transport and the C.B.C. I can assure the hon. member that the problem of the area to which he refers is receiving careful and detailed study at the moment and I believe he will be reasonably well satisfied with the progress that will be made there in the not too distant future.

Thank you, very much. One of the recommendations of the Fowler commission which the minister mentioned in the house was that the dominion network be allowed to lapse. I wonder if that is the intention? I hope it is not. If the two networks continue I wonder if it would be possible for the C.B.C. to give a fairly hard figure as to what it would cost to annually pipe through dominion programs to small communities now receiving trans-Canada programs so they would have both. In other words they would be provided with a choice of program.

I am advised the cost would be very high indeed. I can also tell the hon. member that no immediate consideration is being given to the question. That is not just an euphemistic term. No consideration is being given at the moment nor will any be given in the immediate future to the abandonment of the dominion network. Certainly

no decision will be taken on that at least until after the new directors of the C.B.C. have been appointed and have had an opportunity of surveying the whole situation and obtaining the advice of their technicians and also, I presume, the board of broadcast governors. If any decision of that nature were contemplated it will be a long while in the future and certainly the house would have ample notice of it before it materialized.
The hon. member for Churchill raised the question of television service in his constituency and also referred to the inadequacy of the radio service which they are presently enjoying. He has pressed me on this matter on various occasions and I have had to give him the same answer I have had to give other hon. members of the committee to the effect that this is a matter within the control of the C.B.C. and within the limits of its funds the C.B.C. is attempting to achieve the best possible distribution.
I am pleased to tell the hon. member that in so far as radio is concerned at any rate immediate developments are taking place with respect to the northern service. We are very hopeful that the radio need will be met in the immediate future. Progress has been made, it is past the planning stage and work is being done. I hope and expect that the hon. member will be reasonably well satisfied with what transpires so far as radio is concerned.
But television is another proposition. It is easy to say that all Canadians should be treated equally and we sympathize and agree with that view but distance certainly makes a vast difference in cost. The cost of extending a microwave system to that area would be prohibitive at the moment and to do it in other ways would also be an expensive proposition. Probably the reason why no private television station has been established there is because it would require an undertaking from the C.B.C. to extend its program service and at the moment the C.B.C. is not financially in a position to deal with the problem. However, we have solved the radio problem, I think. Next winter, after the board has been appointed and the C.B.C. has been reconstituted, I am sure whoever happens to be the minister responsible for the C.B.C. at that time will have pressure brought to bear on him again by the hon. member for Churchill to do something for his area which is badly in need of television service as every one realizes.
I wish to be perfectly frank with the hon. member and tell him there are no immediate plans. I would almost go further and say there is no immediate hope of solving the television problem at this time in that area.

Mr. Chairman, there has been much talk recently about the construction of a new building in Montreal which will house all the services of the C.B.C. in that city and also as to the site of that new building. I wonder if the minister is in a position to tell the committee if he is contemplating the construction of such a building and, if so, if an agreement has been reached as to the site of that building?

Mr. Chairman, the minister has a very voluminous mail at all times and one of the matters which has added to the volume has been the number of people in and around Montreal who have written the minister advising him that they have the only available land for the C.B.C. and that it is an excellent buy and should be bought at once. But seriously, there has been no agreement entered into with respect to the purchase of land though, as I have said, many sites have been offered. The C.B.C. has investigated and will continue to investigate any lands offered for sale but no decision has been made. The need is known to the C.B.C., to me and to the government and there is included in these capital estimates, we hope, sufficient moneys with which to purchase the land during the coming year if the committee sees fit to pass these estimates and if the C.B.C. is satisfied as to the availability and price of the land.
I should like to tell the minister there is still much land available in the constituency of Dollard not too far from the national film board and we would welcome such a building.

I hate to come back to the question of low power relay stations but I feel I must. I think we have nine in my constituency and we hope to make it eleven. The cost figure given by the C.B.C. for these low power relay transmitters ranged between $800 and $1,300. The installation costs range between $3,500 and $6,500. I have talked with telegraph men in several communities involved and they say all that is necessary to allow them to broadcast is a simple turn of the switch. I am prepared to accept the explanation.
Let us get to this other request that I have had from the nine communities involved. They want to know why they cannot have the dominion network programs rather than the trans-Canada programs. It is a matter of opinion, but generally the dominion network programs are lighter and more popular with the people. Several times the man in charge of the relay has thrown the switch and sent out the dominion network programs. He has
Supply-C.B.C.
been checked up for it later. Those switches have won a great deal of popular support in the community.
One of the other points I would like to bring up is in connection with the low-power relay stations. I have had requests from two communities which would like to know whether they can use the low-power relay transmitter to make local announcements when the station is not broadcasting or at the end of its schedule or before the schedule begins. They would like to know whether they can make public announcements in relation to things going on in the community; they wondered whether some sort of regulations could be worked out that would allow this and perhaps they could even pay for the time.

Perhaps I have to revise my statement about giving consideration to putting another station in there in the immediate future. The hon. member tells me he has nine in his constituency, which I think is more than any other member in the house has. Perhaps he has too many now. We may have to give consideration to changing some and putting them in other places.
As far as changing from the trans-Canada to the dominion is concerned, I am told by the corporation officials that this is impossible. We have a national network. The trans-Canada facilities are there. To make a change such as the hon. member suggests would involve an expenditure of money such as- well, we would have to sell those nine low-power stations he has there to find money to pay for it, and I am sure he would not want that.
It is true the cost of installing those low-power stations is not great. I was bothered about that. I understand the cost of installing is, as he said, from $800 to several thousand dollars. I would say that what he and some of his friends have overlooked is that it is no good to instal them unless you get the programs. When we get programs that are under contract with the communications system we have to pay so much a mile for the programs, and the farther away the relay station is the more the corporation has to pay, and that is where the cost comes in. It is not the installing of the low-power relay but the operation of it afterwards, under the contract that we have with the communications system which is carrying the program at the time. If it is, say, 10 miles away, that is one thing. If it is 50 miles or 100 miles away, the cost goes up proportionately, and the cost is given in the contract for each one of those low-power relays. You cannot say you can carry it in this way, and so on. That

Supply-C.B.C.
is the cost of the operation and that is why it is more difficult. The more we have to instal the more costly it is.

In view of the fact that the province of Newfoundland is not included in the microwave network-I understand it is the only province in Canada not included in the network-will the minister tell the committee at this time when this handicap of our province will be overcome and when the microwave network will be put through to Newfoundland? In St. John's we have one of the finest independent television stations in Canada. However, it is operating under a handicap in so far as it is not connected with the national network because the microwave does not reach Newfoundland.
One other question; perhaps the minister can advise the house as to the capital expenditure the corporation has planned for the province of Newfoundland in the ensuing year?

Mr. Chairman, I can tell the hon. member for St. John's East, as he knows, that the television microwave expenditure is being proceeded with. Unfortunately there have been delays in the acquisition of material. I had thought that the whole thing would be completed within the next few months but there have been substantial delays owing to material shortages. As a result, I do not think he can expect to see the completion of that microwave system until sometime early next summer. It may be that late. It certainly will not be, as I expected it would be, early in the winter, but it is going ahead. All the troubles are now settled and the material is ordered, and he can confidently look forward to the microwave sometime during the next summer months, and I hope early in the summer.
In so far as the capital budget is concerned, we have the cost of the microwave station and I think that is all that is really included in the capital budget. It depends, of course, on many things. The general budget for the country as a whole is not earmarked, and it will depend on expenditures in different places and how much money is available as to what is done.

Mr. Chairman, once again I would like to bring to the attention of the minister a problem concerning a radio station that exists in my riding. I am referring to the C.B.C. station known as CBY, which operates on 790 kilocycles in the city of Corner Brook in the province of Newfoundland. This radio station, now operated by C.B.C., was formerly operated on the west coast of Newfoundland long before Newfoundland came into confederation, and its programs, both local and otherwise, were broadcast all along the

west coast of Newfoundland. In an area where communications leave a lot to be desired, radio services become much more important under such circumstances. The result is that this radio station has become very important to the people on the west coast of Newfoundland in so far as local news bulletins, news about fishing boats up and down the coast, and so forth, are concerned.
This section of the coast is about 300 miles long. The station is situated approximately 100 miles from the southern end and 200 miles from the northern end. Over the years this station has given very fine service to the area. Of late, however, in the southern part and in the northern part interference from station CKEC at Newcastle, New Brunswick has been experienced. The trouble appears to be that the station at Newcastle is on exactly the same frequency as the station at Corner Brook.
I must make myself clear to the minister. I am not making any complaints about the station at Newcastle and I wish to say right now that as far as I know the interference to which I am referring does not exist within the protected area of CKEC at Newcastle and neither, I think, does it appear within the protected area of CBY. The northern part of the west coast of Newfoundland and the southern part are both outside the protected area but at the same time they are areas that have been served for a number of years by this station at Corner Brook. This interference from CKEC is such that the local station at Corner Brook cannot be heard.
As I said before, over the years this station has given a very fine contribution. It is operated by a very efficient manager, supported by a very capable staff. I say that because of the fact they have been able to play a great part in the local programs in the area and today the people look to it a good deal. When I think of the people in the northern part of the northern peninsula and in the southern part where they are no longer able to get the programs that are broadcast from the station I begin to wonder just what can be done about it. I think the frequency which has been allocated to CKEC is quite within the legal authority of the international code for assigning frequencies, and I have no doubt that from a legal point of view those two stations are quite within their rights. I believe, too, that from an engineering point of view those two stations are perfectly all right.
I agree that the thing may be right legally and I agree that it may be right mechanically but there is something wrong if the people of an area have been able to enjoy these programs from the station over a long period of

years and now can no longer do so. What can be done about it, of course, is a matter for an engineer. It may be a question of increasing the power or of changing the frequency. It may be a problem of changing the antennae or ground patterns. Whatever the problem is, I suggest to the minister that he would be doing a service to these people in the northern part of Newfoundland if something could be done to solve it. I might also ask the minister to give any information he can when he is replying about what is happening in the city of Corner Brook as far as television coverage is concerned.

With respect to the frequency problem to which the hon. member has referred, it is a most unfortunate circumstance that an area which enjoyed radio reception for many years has now apparently had its reception severely prejudiced or has practically lost it entirely due to the allocation of a wavelength somewhere else. Of course, that has happened in other places. As the hon. member says, there is no question about the legality of it. These frequencies were allocated by the Department of Transport in accordance with the international agreement. As the hon. member knows, something happened and although, as he says, the areas directly concerned are clear, you have these other areas which have enjoyed radio reception for years and are now being severely interfered with. The departmental officials tell me that they have been attempting to cope with the situation. Studies have been going on and investigations are being made. Frankly, no solution has yet been reached but I can assure the hon. member that I will urge the C.B.C. to pursue the matter and I am sure they will take every step possible to attain a solution of this nasty and difficult problem with which he is confronted.
So far as the question of television in Corner Brook is concerned, I am not sure what the exact status is at the moment. It is expected, I am told, that there will be sufficient moneys in the capital vote this year to provide for that area.

On June 25 the minister
announced in the house proposals for surveys of the possibilities of the establishment of six satellite television stations in Canada, including one in Trail. Can the minister inform the house how far the surveys have proceeded with respect to the establishment of the one in Trail?

Mr. Chairman, I know that last June the minister announced that there would be a French language satellite station in Winnipeg to serve the French population in the west. Will the change in the set-up and the creation of a new board delay the
Supply-C.B.C.
project? I know that the people of Manitoba and particularly of my riding of St. Boniface are much interested in a French station in Manitoba. I believe that there are now about two hours a week in French on the Winnipeg station and although many English speaking people enjoy French programs there are always a few who prefer to have all the programs in English. If there were a French station they would not be deprived of all English programs by the two hours in French on the local station. I also understand that many of the students taking French at the university would be interested in listening to French programs over a French station. I would appreciate it very much if the minister would assure the people of Manitoba that this project will not be delayed because of the new board being set up.

I can give the assurance that it is not going to be delayed because of the proposed changes in the broadcasting bill we passed yesterday. The situation with respect to Trail and the situation with respect to St. Boniface are practically identical. Surveys are being made and are virtually completed. Engineering designs are going ahead for the locations and in both cases work will be started this year. It will not be completed this year but I am quite sure it will be fairly early next year. Some time next year in any event the stations at Trail and St. Boniface will be completed and in operation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 56 carry?

Before the item carries, Mr. Chairman, I cannot refrain from pointing out that the debate this afternoon, and I am not seeking to criticize anyone on either side of the house for it, is the best possible illustration of the unwisdom of the decision made yesterday. We have listened all afternoon to members getting up and urging the government to do something about a system that we thought and still think should be independent of the government. This business of having annual appropriations, which is what we are talking about now, for the C.B.C. instead of having the C.B.C. discussed in a committee in the way the C.N.R. is discussed is, it seems to me, a very retrograde step indeed.

I do not want to get into another altercation with the hon. gentleman. I know that at one time he was busy running a department and probably like other cabinet ministers then and cabinet ministers today did not spend as much time in the house as he does now as a private member. However, I sat in the house for 10 years as a private member and the practice that has been going on this afternoon has gone on every time the C.B.C. vote has come up in the past

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration 10 years. There is no difference whatsoever. Members of the house who had requests to make made them and the situation has not changed. Of course, any reference to the debate on the bill passed yesterday is completely out of order.
I might point out-
I knew you would.
-that there have not been annual appropriations except for the last two or three years so that the minister's statement about the last 10 years is not correct.
It does not make any difference. Requests were made just the same.

There used to be debates on setting up radio committees when hon. members expressed their views about what they would like the C.B.C. to do and that is as it should be, but this business of having to appeal to the government is what we find objectionable.
Mr. Chairman, I simply wish to say that I do not want to have us identified with the views expressed by the very partisan member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: This completes the estimates of the Department of National Revenue.

65. To provide, subject to the approval of treasury board, for trans-oceanic and inland transportation and other assistance for immigrants and settlers, including care en route and while awaiting employment; and to provide further for payments to the provinces pursuant to agreements entered1 into, with the approval of the governor in council, in respect of expenses incurred by the provinces for indigent immigrants, $8,180,000.

Mr. Chairman, when we were last in committee on these estimates we were considering vote No. 65 and I did not have the opportunity on that occasion to make some reference to this vote and to the size of it. Since the estimates were prepared some time last autumn there have been changes in circumstances which make it possible now to reduce the amount of this vote. Accordingly, I would ask my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, to move this reduction. I should like to have the amount of the vote reduced by $500,000.

I move:
That vote 65, immigration branch, to provide subject to the approval of treasury board, for trans-oceanic and inland transportation and other assistance for immigrants and settlers, including care en route and while awaiting employment, etc., be reduced by $500,000.
I wonder if the hon. lady would explain to us how she came to make this shockingly bad estimate?

At the time that the estimates were drawn up we had expected we would have a great many more people on subsistence than now appears to be the case. We have been able to procure employment for so many refugees and others who were formerly on assistance that it is now possible to make this reduction in the estimates.

That is a very encouraging statement indeed, by the hon. lady. The other day I meant to ask, but I did not think of it, how many people are on subsistence at the present time? I shall put two or three related questions because it will be easier to answer them that way. How many persons are receiving subsistence? How many of those persons are seeking employment? How much has been spent in total on subsistence by the department so far in the present fiscal year or, if the hon. lady has not an up-to-date figure for the calendar year, whatever would be a convenient recent date?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Would the committee be prepared to accept the amendment at this stage?
Agreed.
Amendment agreed to.
As of August 15, Mr. Chairman, the total number of immigrants receiving subsistence was 1,033; the total number of workers yet unplaced or the total number seeking work was 323.
That includes Hungarians?
Yes; as a matter of fact, of that number 98 are Hungarians and 225 are others. The amount to the end of July, for which the hon. member asked, is $2,140,713.97.
From what date?
For the fiscal year.
Since April 1?
Oh yes.

I must say that I think what the minister has just told us is quite a tribute to the efficiency of the staff who look after these matters in the immigration branch. I am sure the hon. lady would today agree with me in that.
The other question I wanted to ask concerns the assisted passage loans. I would be interested to know whether or not assisted passage loans are still being made, to what classes of persons they are being made at the present time, and also what the latest balance sheet shows on the assisted passage fund?

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration

The total number admitted in the first six months of the calendar year, to the end of June, was 4,962. On their behalf there was paid $1,329,874. In the same period, we received repayment or there were collections amounting to $1,797,665. The hon. gentleman asked about the condition of the fund, I think, and also the classes of persons.

Yes, that is right. Perhaps I could make it a little more precise. I should like to know the total amount of loans since this scheme was started, the total amount repaid and the total amount outstanding as of the latest convenient date?

Assistance has been given to 107,092 since February 1, 1951, and the total amount paid amounted to $17,181,040. Collections have amounted to $10,963,616. A rapid calculation would indicate that there is something over $6 million outstanding.
No, I will not ask the hon. lady to do the subtraction. Can she give the categories of persons receiving the loans?

Roughly speaking, Mr. Chairman, there are those who are coming to take occupations and those who are in need of assistance, not sponsored by relatives, but those who are coming here to take employment and who have indicated that they are unable to pay their own passage.

I am not going to detain the committee, but I have tried several devices to find out from the hon. lady what categories of persons are admitted to take employment in this country. She tabled a very complicated chart which I never quite understood when I was minister, and I frankly confess I do not understand now. Perhaps some day she would have some one of the officials in her department translate it into either English or French as a list of occupations, in any kind of order at all, but in plain, ordinary words that we could understand, and lay it on the table. I shall not detain her now.

In the same spirit of good will, may I say that I agree it is a complicated document. On the other hand, as the hon. member knows, an occupation in which there may be no vacancies in one part of the country may show unfilled vacancies in another part of the country, and when you try to signify by area and also by occupation precisely what classes are open, it does become complicated.

I will let the hon. lady off if she will just give a list of all the occupations to which immigrants are admitted in any part of the country?
57071-3-266
Does the hon. member mean right now?
Oh, no, by no means, but before the end of the session.
All right, I will.
Could the minister tell the committee, of those immigrants who are receiving assistance, how many were admitted to Canada without jobs waiting or guaranteed for them?

I do not believe we would have that information without tracing down every single one of these persons and finding out what the circumstances were under which they entered the country. It is conceivable that a person would come in to take employment, and then within the first year have that employment disappear. He might come in as a person destined for a specific job, and still receive subsistence later on.
Could the minister tell us whether there is any priority or any special consideration given to immigrants who apply to enter Canada and who have a job guaranteed to them on arrival?

I doubt whether we can guarantee jobs, or whether we can indicate to immigrants the possibility of securing employment in certain places or at certain times. The possible exception might be if one comes out to take a job on a specific farm or in a specific household as a domestic. I am not sure that I understand the hon. member's question.

I think the minister misunderstood my question. My question was this. Is there any priority or special consideration given to an applicant to migrate to Canada who has already a job assured to him on arrival by his relatives or some other people?

If I understand the hon. member's question now, what he means is this. Suppose he is assured of employment here in a specific position but has not the necessary funds to come out, will he be assisted in passage?

I am not speaking of assistance in passage. I am speaking of an immigrant who applies to migrate to Canada and who has a job assured to him on arrival. He may come on his own steam, but he has a job assured him on arrival. I am asking whether any preference or special consideration is given to such an immigrant over one who has no job waiting for him on arrival and who subsequently requires the assistance of the government.
4206	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
The hon. member gets me confused by adding at the end of his question the words "assistance of the government".

I do not mean to confuse the minister, Mr. Chairman. If I may repeat my question, I shall do so. Suppose a person applies to migrate to Canada, has a job assured him on arrival either by relatives or friends and pays his own expenses. Is there any priority or special consideration given to such an applicant over one who has no job waiting for him and who may become a charge to the government?

The answer to that question would be that, if the position to which he is destined is one for which there are no applicants in Canada and it has been cleared as such through the national employment service, his entry would be expedited; yes.

May I ask the minister this question. Does that apply to relatives of Chinese citizens who make application for their relatives to come here and who in every case have assured employment, who never come on the community for care or are never any expense to the Canadian people or the Canadian government?
No. That does not apply to sponsored cases.

First I should like to compliment the minister on being willing to make and in fact arranging for an amendment reducing an estimate. That is quite a favourable action in comparison to that of a minister who some days ago insisted on an estimate for parliamentary assistants remaining, even though the possibility of the estimate being used had been exhausted by the passage of the months. However, I wonder whether the minister could give us a breakdown as between the various purposes for which the estimate of, I now take it, $7,680,000 is expected to be used? I notice that in the details even less information is given than is given at page 12 of the blue book. What I should like to know is this. What is the estimate that will be needed for trans-oceanic transportation assistance; what is the estimate that will be needed for inland transportation assistance; what is the estimate for other assistance for immigrants and settlers; and what is the estimate for maintenance of immigrants who have not the wherewithal to look after themselves once they are in Canada?

I think I can give the hon. member the broad breakdown. Inland transportation is estimated at $640,000; transoceanic transportation, $720,000; food, shelter and incidental expenses, $3,800,000. That is


the one that will be reduced by half a million dollars. Then there is family assistance for immigrants and settlers, $2,800,000; and federal-provincial agreement, $220,000.

The other day I noticed a news item about Canada accepting another limited number of refugees of the revolt in Hungary. Might I ask the minister this question. Have all these refugees now been placed somewhere in the world or are there large camps of refugees remaining in Austria or Yugoslavia or elsewhere? I believe there were some in the other western European countries.
It is hoped that this movement will clear up the Hungarian refugees who have been in camps in various places.
The minister says that she expects that this large admission to Canada-
And to other countries.

-is likely to end the matter as far as Canada is concerned. I have one other question. Even with the reduction of the minister's estimates, I notice that it still leaves $7 J million compared to the $12,911,000 for the fiscal year ended last March 31. I noticed a news report the other day that we were expecting to Canada this year only in the neighbourhood of 70,000 immigrants which figure I believe is only roughly 35 per cent of what it was a year ago.
There were that many in the first six months, practically.

I wonder whether I could ask the hon. lady a question. How many settlers who were not immigrants received assistance since the item was changed to include settlers? Perhaps the hon. lady does not know what a settler is. I may say that a settler is a Canadian citizen who left Canada a long time ago and came back. We changed the law a couple of years ago so that for this purpose they could be treated as immigrants. This question is asked perhaps just out of idle curiosity. If the figure is not readily available, I would not press the matter.

I do not have it right here but I shall be glad to get it for the hon. gentleman.
While I am on my feet may I correct a statement I made a few moments ago. Amongst those for whom assisted passages are available are wives and minor children. I said no sponsored relatives were eligible but wives and minor children in Europe sponsored by residents of Canada are also eligible for assisted passage.

There is just one other question that I should like to ask the hon. lady. In response to a question I asked earlier in the session she gave me a categorical assurance that a settlement made with the government of Ontario with respect to Hungarian refugees was in no respect whatsoever more favourable than the settlement made with Saskatchewan. I should* like to be quite sure that was the case.

If my memory serves me well, I did not put it in quite that way. I think I said that the one was based on the same general principle as the other. I would not be able to answer the hon. gentleman if he is asking me if there was any particular in which the one is more favourable than the other. I would have to inquire.

If the hon. lady has examined the file at all carefully she will recall that there was a good deal of negotiation that went on about this point before she became minister and before the government changed, and that I took the view that we could not possibly give more favourable treatment to a wealthy province like Ontario than we were giving to Saskatchewan. It was because I took that attitude that the negotiation broke down and no settlement was ever reached with the government of Ontario. I think we really ought to be assured in the committee before the estimates are passed that all provinces-and of course Ontario and Saskatchewan were the ones that performed the widest services in this field-were treated on a basis of absolute equality.
I will try to get that information for the hon. member.
If the hon. lady would undertake to give her reply tomorrow I will not hold up the item on that account.
Very well. With respect to the question asked about settlers, as of July 31, 89 settlers received transportation assistance in order to return to Canada.
Would the minister say if any preference whatsoever is given to applicants when the sponsor is prepared to post a bond or give a guarantee that the immigrant will never become a public charge?

I think I am correct in saying that we do not ask for a bond except where there may be health conditions indicating that the person could be a public charge. These cases are handled so carefully and individually that I do not think I could give a general answer to that question.

I wish to make a few general observations. My views on the urgency of 57071-3-2661
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration increasing immigration to Canada have been stated in this house over the years since I have been sitting here and those views have been supported in large measure by eminent members of the house. If I might mention the Hon. George Drew, the present Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister himself; all those gentlemen have taken views similar to my own and have stressed the importance of admitting immigrants and expanding our population. I do not wish to go over the ground again but there is one phase of it which I would like to draw to the attention of the minister and that is the expediting of immigration into Canada of the close relatives of people already here.
This is a very delicate subject and I think merits all the sympathetic consideration of the minister. I know that in the past I have found great sympathy on the part of the former minister and the officials of the department when dealing with the cases of close relatives, and I wonder if since immigration has been stopped, generally speaking, this has not influenced the immigration of close relatives, although I understand such immigration has not been stopped by the present government.
I personally know of a great many people who have close relatives abroad and who were delighted by the fact that a lady had been appointed as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration for the first time in Canada's history. They felt, quite rightly, that this lady would understand with more sympathy the close ties of family life and the great urgency of having relatives close at hand. I would like to address myself to the minister with a simple plea that she could perhaps avoid being influenced by the men around her who are also sympathetic, but who are more inclined to adhere to the strict interpretation of the regulations. These are men whose judgment I have always respected and by whose decisions I have always abided, but yet I feel that sometimes as supporting officials to the minister, without the authority or the right enjoyed by the minister, they cannot extend sympathetic consideration to these cases. I therefore appeal to the minister as warmly and as urgently as I can to extend every possible human sympathy to these cases concerning close relatives and to even go a little beyond the strict interpretation of the letter of the law and to apply the sympathy which should come from a minister of this department,, especially from a lady whose sympathy and kindness is known.

I thank the hon. gentleman for his kind remarks. The policy of the department is of course to keep family groups together, but when the hon. gentleman speaks about immigration having been curtailed this

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration year I must say that the vast majority of those who have come to Canada have been people sponsored by their relatives in this country.
I think 1 am correct in saying that this department has always lent a sympathetic ear to those persons who find themselves parted from their immediate relatives by reason of their migration to Canada or for other reasons beyond their control. It is our hope that we can bring these family groups together, but when I say that I cannot guarantee that this would be a blanket policy applied to all parts of the globe because, as the hon. member knows, different conditions prevail in different countries and different areas.
In so far as possible we do hope to bring family groups together, although we cannot always do this as quickly as we would like, for many reasons. I can assure the hon. member that the policy is undergoing close scrutiny at the present time and we hope to have an announcement to make in that respect in the not too distant future, bearing in mind just such circumstances as those he has described.

I am a little hard of hearing sometimes but did I hear the minister correctly to the effect that of this roughly $7 million, $3,800,000 was for incidentals? Would she clarify what she said. I know there were other matters, but I was not quite clear in that respect.
That was for food, shelter and incidental expenses. Incidentals would be just a very small portion of that.

Would the minister explain how this is a separate item from the next item-family assistance of $2,800,000? This was the sum of money paid by agreement with the provinces. Exactly how does the item for food come under $3,800,000 and the family assistance under $2,800,000?

Mr. Chairman, family
assistance is the term given to family allowances when paid to immigrants who would not, by reason of their short term of residence in this country, qualify for family allowances. There might be, and in my opinion there is, some room for argument as to whether this might not properly be paid by the Department of National Health and Welfare, but that is a matter of conjecture. Nevertheless, that is what it is, family allowances paid on behalf of the children of immigrants.

May I make a general remark on this item. I believe the basic responsibility of the department should be to find proper immigrants for Canada and I say

that when over $7 million out of $18 million is used for the bringing of immigrants to Canada and the maintenance of those immigrants, that is a fairly high proportion. Relatively more money should be spent in finding ways and means to let Canada have those people who so badly want to come here and who will not be a burden to the Canadian taxpayers.

Mr. Chairman, as I wish to make somewhat extended remarks on this item, may I call it six o'clock?
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.
